In brief

In Circe a hallucinatory Buck Mulligan suddenly appears "From the top of a tower" and comments on Stephen's dead mother suddenly appearing from beneath the floorboards: "She's beastly dead. The pity of it! Mulligan meets the afflicted mother." This tableau recapitulates the conversation between the two men in Telemachus, and "afflicted mother" seems an apt description of Stephen's mother. The phrase, however, is one that Oliver Gogarty used to describe his own mother, and there is reason to suppose that Mrs. Gogarty felt afflicted not only by her own health problems but also by her son's friendship with James Joyce. The ambiguous reference, and its religious provenance—the Catholic Stations of the Cross—mean that not just one loving mother but two of them are joined in condemning Stephen's heinous apostasy.

At more length

Ellmann's biography recounts "a story current in Dublin that Gogarty, returning home late one night during his medical course, staggered up the steps of his home on Rutland Square, reciting a station of the Cross at each step until, as he reached the top of the stairs and his worried mother opened the door, he concluded, 'Gogarty meets the afflicted mother'" (366). In the Fourth Station of the Cross, as Jesus carries his cross to Calvary, he sees his mother Mary in the crowd lining the street. No words are exchanged, only looks brimming with emotion. It is a moment of profound, shared suffering.

Joyce was all too familar with his friend's habit of casting himself as a suffering Christ. In Telemachus he has Mulligan say, while doffing his dressing gown, "Mulligan is stripped of his garments." In Circe he quotes another of these mocking meditations a moment after "Stephen's mother, emaciated, rises stark through the floor, in leper grey with a wreath of faded orangeblossoms and a torn bridal veil, her face worn and noseless, green with gravemould." Since Mulligan has gaily told Stephen, in the first chapter, that "The aunt thinks you killed your mother," it would seem that his second invocation of the Stations of the Cross must refer to May Goulding Dedalus. She certainly has been afflicted—abused by her alcoholic husband, let down by her apostate son, devoured by her terminal cancer.

But since the biblical scene concerns a suffering son meeting his equally afflicted mother, and since Gogarty was famed for putting it to precisely that use, one may wonder whether something more may be going on in the allusion. Gogarty's mother Margaret died in 1906 after several years of suffering due to bronchitis and emphysema. And there is more: in a page on James Joyce Online Notes Terence Killeen shows that she was also troubled by some psychological suffering due to her son consorting with wicked friends.

On 30 December 1903 Mrs. Gogarty wrote to Thomas Kettle, one of Joyce's college acquaintances, asking him to come visit "us" at Rutland Square and talk about her son. "You can do him an inestimable service by your companionship and advice," the letter suggests, "to counteract the evil effects of others, one, especially, a bad Catholic who spent a great deal of time with Oliver last winter before I discovered he was, or pretended to be, an Agnostic, so I forbade him to call here any more."

A few days later, on 1 January 1904, Mrs. Gogarty wrote Kettle again, urging him a second time to come and "give me great counsel about Oliver, that erratic being whom I cannot control." Gogarty respects him, she says, so he might be able to "counteract the influences to which he is subjected." She says, "I have a horror of Mr George Moore whom he meets at Sir Thornley Stoker’s, whither he has gone this evening." But as Moore declared in 1903 that he had converted from Catholicism to Protestantism, he could hardly be the declared "Agnostic" mentioned in the first letter.

Killeen comments, "I think we need be in little doubt as to who the 'bad Catholic' is. This letter, like the other one apparently overlooked by biographers, may well give some indication of the nature of the 'call' that Mulligan says his aunt intends to make on Stephen’s father and it does make the possibility of such a call, or maybe a letter, more plausible. It is not unlikely that when Mrs Gogarty, in the first letter cited, mentions the possibility of Kettle meeting 'us', the 'us' refers to her and to Gogarty's aunt, given that Gogarty's father, Dr Henry Gogarty, was no longer alive at this time. Mulligan's aunt, of course, herself features strongly in Ulysses. It also, incidentally, indicates that Joyce probably did frequent Gogarty’s house to some extent, making the scene of Mulligan telling his mother that Stephen’s mother is 'beastly dead' more plausible as well."

If Killeen is right about the identity of the Agnostic and about the two sisters' reason for wanting to remove Oliver Gogarty from the evil influence of James Joyce, then the double reference of "the afflicted mother" makes a whole new kind of sense—one that is highly relevant to the scene in Circe where a ghoulish May Goulding Dedalus visits her son and demands that he "Repent! O, the fire of hell!" As good Catholics, both mothers believe that leaving the bosom of Mother Church is the surest ticket to an eternity of fiery torture. Relentless lighthearted mockery of every article of Christian faith, such as Gogarty and Mulligan delight in, is bad enough. Outright disbelief and defiance are infinitely worse. This is the fiercely uncompromising Catholicism that Stephen has desperately renounced. Mulligan may make light of the disagreement in Oxen of the Sun, saying, "Aunty mine's writing Pa Kinch. Baddybad Stephen lead astray goodygood Malachi." But for Stephen it is a matter of life and death. 

John Hunt 2026
